fact_check_log.claim: Samoa's tourism authority describes Samoan culture as based on fa'a Samoa, translated as 'The Samoan Way', which is holistic and, for many, closely associated with honouring one's family.

Samoan society is organised by extended families (aiga), each with its own Matai ('chief' or 'leader') titles connected to districts, villages and family land, a system the tourism authority calls 'fa
Matai are responsible for administrative duties and for maintaining the traditions and customs of the village, and their status is highly respected.
Members of the aiga are expected to be generous and to put the interests of the group or community ahead of their own.
In village areas local law prevails and can vary from village to village.

Britannica says Samoans have strived to preserve the fa'a Samoa ('Samoan way of life'), so many traditions of rural life remain virtually unchanged, though some customs have changed markedly, particul
Most Samoan villages have a church and a meetinghouse, which doubles as a cultural centre.
Matai are still expected to deliver rhythmic and poetical orations at council meetings and other major events.
Samoans often entertain one another at weddings and other family gatherings with ula, in which two groups alternate between singing and dancing.
Kava, a traditional nonalcoholic drink from a tropical pepper plant, is consumed at social events, mainly by matai.

Samoans readily adopted Christianity after European contact and even remote villages built churches, often of grand proportions; the Congregational Christian Church of Samoa is the dominant church, wi
Tens of thousands of Samoans have emigrated to New Zealand, the United States, Australia and elsewhere.

Te Papa describes 'ie toga (fine mat) as presented as a valuable in ceremonies that cement relationships between people, and as worn as a garment on important occasions by high-ranking matai and taupo
'Ie toga are the highest-ranking item in the Samoan exchange system; they seal relationships between groups of people and feature at special events and ceremonies.

An 'ie toga is hand woven with fibres so fine that it could take months or years to complete; in the past they were made by young women, who also completed mats left unfinished by older female relativ
'Ie toga are preserved with great care, some pass through several generations gaining sentimental or historical value, and they may be given names.
Te Papa says that in Samoan marriage ceremonies 'ie tōga are presented to the husband's family by the bride's family.
Te Papa records an 1800s 'ie tōga woven from pandanus (Pandanus tectorius) with red feathers.
'Ie tōga are exchanged frequently and can pass through generations, and a particularly old and fine one brings great dignity to a ceremony.

At a 2002 presentation of the 'ie tōga Le Ageagea o Tumua, a Samoan orator's published speech referred to villages 'chanting the marriage chants' and presented the fine mat 'to seal our marriage' betw
Each of Samoa's several thousand aiga (extended families) designates at least one matai to lead and represent it, and the matai form village councils to administer local affairs.
Te Ara, the New Zealand government encyclopedia, says the bedrock of fa‘asamoa (Samoan culture) is aiga (family), which remains a permanent fixture.
Te Ara notes that for New Zealand-born Samoans the church often provides the anchor, and Samoans tend to return to their ethnic identity when they mature and have children.

Te Papa's Pacific curator writes that the tulāfale (orator), through lāuga (oratory), represents the interests of ali‘i at formal occasions and is the mouthpiece of families, villages and districts, i
Tulāfale are keepers of cultural knowledge such as history and genealogies, and negotiate the relationships between different parties.

Tulāfale usually present lāuga indoors in a fale or outdoors on the malae (village green), and carry the fue (fly whisk), to‘oto‘o (staff) and wear the ‘ulafala (pandanus key necklace) as symbols of t
UNESCO's Samoa state page lists one element inscribed: 'Ie Samoa, fine mat and its cultural value, 2019, Representative List (RL).
